trial_name: HACA — Mild Therapeutic Hypothermia After Cardiac Arrest (2002)
citation: Hypothermia after Cardiac Arrest Study Group. Mild therapeutic hypothermia to improve the neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest. N Engl J Med. 2002;346(8):549-556
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, open-label, blinded outcome assessment
one_liner: Induced mild hypothermia (32–34°C) for 24 h improved favorable neurological outcome (55% vs 39%; RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.08–1.81) and reduced mortality (41% vs 55%) at 6 months in comatose survivors of witnessed shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

pico.population: Adults (18–75 y) comatose after witnessed out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest, with specific time windows (bystander BLS 5–15 min, EMS attempt 15–60 min, ROSC ≤60 min, stable MAP/oxygenation)
pico.intervention: Induced mild hypothermia to 32–34°C (bladder temp) for 24 h using external cooling (TheraKool) ± ice packs and cold fluids (4°C Ringer’s lactate 30 mL/kg up to 2 L); sedation with midazolam/fentanyl + pancuronium paralysis
pico.comparison: Standard ICU care with normothermia; no protocolised temperature management in control group
pico.outcome: Favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1–2) at 6 months

background.existing_knowledge: Comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest frequently died or had severe neurological disability due to global cerebral ischaemia–reperfusion injury. Experimental and early clinical data suggested that mild hypothermia could attenuate reperfusion injury.
background.knowledge_gap: High-quality randomised evidence in adults was lacking; post-resuscitation fever was increasingly recognized as potentially harmful.
background.hypothesis: Induced mild hypothermia (32–34°C) would increase the proportion with CPC 1–2 at 6 months and reduce mortality, without materially increasing complications.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment.
methods.setting: Multiple centres across Europe (exact number not stated in scraped summary); patients admitted to ICU after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

inclusion: Interval collapse to bystander BLS 5–15 min
Interval collapse to EMS attempt 15–60 min
Persistent coma (no verbal response) after ROSC
exclusion: Coma before arrest due to CNS depressants
Response to verbal commands before randomisation
MAP <60 mmHg for >30 min after ROSC
Oxygen saturation <85% for >15 min after ROSC
Arrest after arrival of emergency personnel

methods.intervention: External cooling with TheraKool device (forced cold air) escalated to ice packs and cold (4°C) Ringer’s lactate if needed. Target bladder temperature 32–34°C. Cooling started as soon as possible after ROSC, aiming for target within 4 h. Cold fluids: Ringer’s lactate 4°C, 30 mL/kg (max 2 L) over 30 min if target not reached. Sedation/shivering: midazolam 0.125 mg/kg/h + fentanyl 0.002 mg/kg/h (adjustable) + pancuronium 0.1 mg/kg every 2 h for 32 h. Maintain 32–34°C for 24 h from start of cooling, then passive rewarming over ~8 h.
methods.comparison: Standard ICU care with normothermia; patients on conventional bed without active cooling. Other post-resuscitation treatments per local practice.
methods.blinding: Treating clinicians unblinded for first 48 h; outcome assessors blinded to group allocation.
methods.sample_size_power: Not reported. Trial stopped early at 275 patients due to funding/slow enrolment.
secondary_outcomes: Complications within 7 days (any, bleeding, pneumonia, sepsis, arrhythmia)
methods.follow_up: 6 months for primary endpoint; in-hospital and 7-day complications recorded.

headline_bullets: Hypothermia increased favorable neurological outcome at 6 months (55% vs 39%; RR 1.40, P=0.009; NNT 6).
Mortality at 6 months was lower with hypothermia (41% vs 55%; RR 0.74, P=0.02; NNT 7).
Median time to target temperature was 8 h after ROSC; 19 patients never reached target, 14 discontinued early.
Overall complications were similar (73% vs 70%), but pneumonia, sepsis, and bleeding were numerically more frequent with hypothermia.

domains.notes: Block randomisation (blocks of 10) stratified by centre using sealed envelopes; concealment beyond envelope process not described.
Open-label for first 48 h; co-interventions and withdrawal decisions could introduce performance bias; outcome assessors were blinded.
Primary outcome missing for 1 patient in each arm (analysed as 75/136 vs 54/137); 14 patients discontinued cooling early (haemodynamic instability 8, bleeding 2, etc.).
19 patients never reached target temperature; median time to target 8 h; 70% required ice packs; crossover not reported.
Groups similar on age and sex; notable imbalances: diabetes 19% vs 8%, coronary heart disease 43% vs 32% (both more in normothermia).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity: randomisation and blinded outcome assessment support causal inference, but open-label delivery, incomplete target attainment, unreported power calculation, and early stopping increase imprecision and bias risk.

domains.notes: Highly selected: only witnessed VF arrests with constrained time windows and post-ROSC stability; excludes nonshockable rhythms, unwitnessed arrests, prolonged downtimes, refractory shock, age >75, pregnancy.

Cooling strategy (external device + ice/cold fluids, sedation, paralysis) is feasible in many ICUs but requires training; results may differ with variations in prehospital times, coronary reperfusion, and prognostication practices.

external_validity.verdict: Limited generalisability to a narrow subset of comatose post-cardiac arrest patients; evidence needed for broader populations (nonshockable rhythms, older age, longer downtimes).

strengths: Randomised controlled design with clinically meaningful functional endpoint (CPC at 6 months)
Blinded outcome assessment, reducing detection bias for primary outcome
Pragmatic ICU-feasible cooling protocol (external cooling + escalation)
Protocolised temperature target and duration (32–34°C for 24 h, rewarming over 8 h)
limitations: Stopped early at 275 patients due to funding/feasibility, risking imprecision and overestimation of effect size
Open-label care with potential for differential co-interventions and prognostication/withdrawal bias
Late attainment of target temperature (median 8 h) and incomplete protocol adherence (19 never reached target)
Control group temperature not protocolised, leaving uncertainty about contribution of induced hypothermia vs. fever avoidance

critical_appraisal.summary: A landmark RCT that demonstrated a clinically important benefit of induced hypothermia in a narrow shockable out-of-hospital arrest cohort, but early stopping, open-label bias, and limited generalisability require cautious interpretation; subsequent trials have refined the role of temperature control.

sections.authors_conclusion: Induced mild hypothermia (32–34°C) for 24 h improved favorable neurological outcome at 6 months (55% vs 39%; RR 1.40, P=0.009) and reduced mortality (41% vs 55%; P=0.02) in comatose survivors of witnessed shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In a restricted cohort (witnessed VF arrest, moderate downtime, early stability), mild hypothermia improves neurological recovery and survival; contemporary practice emphasizes active temperature control and fever prevention with a target temperature (e.g., 32–36°C) tailored to the patient.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Comatose adults after witnessed shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with short to moderate downtimes and early post-ROSC hemodynamic/oxygenation stability.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That all post-cardiac arrest patients should be cooled to 32–34°C; later trials suggest no clear benefit of 33°C over 36°C when fever is avoided.
implementation_caveats: Requires reliable temperature monitoring and shivering control (sedation/paralysis)
Delayed initiation (e.g., beyond ROSC+8 h) may reduce benefit
Complications like pneumonia, sepsis, and bleeding may be more frequent, warranting vigilant surveillance

controversies.notes: Not explicitly discussed for HACA, but subsequent trials debated optimal composite endpoints for post-arrest studies.
Correspondence highlighted that the eligible cohort was a minority of screened patients; restrictive rhythm and timing criteria limit inference to broader arrest populations.

controversies.topic: Baseline neurological severity and prognostic balance
controversies.notes: Limited reporting of coma depth at enrolment raised concern about residual prognostic imbalance despite randomisation.

controversies.topic: Metabolic and fluid effects of cooling
controversies.notes: Hypothermia was associated with lower potassium levels (median 3.5 vs 3.7 mmol/L at 24 h; 4.0 vs 4.4 at 48 h), higher fluid volumes (10.7 vs 8.8 L), and more positive fluid balance (5.6 vs 4.2 L).
Subsequent RCTs comparing 33°C vs 36°C (TTM) did not show superiority of 33°C, challenging a ‘lower is better’ interpretation.
A later RCT (HYPERION) in nonshockable rhythms reported improved neurological outcome with hypothermia, but overall evidence remains heterogeneous by rhythm and setting.

A large contemporary RCT (TTM2) comparing hypothermia to targeted normothermia with active fever prevention did not show improved outcomes with hypothermia and reported more arrhythmias causing haemodynamic compromise.

Modern guidance shifted from routine 32–34°C for all eligible patients to active temperature control with fever prevention, selecting a target temperature (e.g., ≤37.5°C or 32–36°C) tailored to context.

Contemporary scientific statements emphasize temperature management as a bundle (continuous monitoring, controlled cooling/normothermia, fever avoidance) rather than a single ‘hypothermia-only’ intervention.
Updated meta-analyses incorporating newer trials have reduced certainty that hypothermia confers mortality or neurological benefit versus active normothermia strategies.

context_related_trials.relation: Compared target temperature 33°C vs 36°C and found no significant difference in mortality or neurological outcome, challenging the HACA conclusion that 32–34°C is superior to normothermia.

Compared hypothermia (33°C) vs active normothermia with fever prevention and found no difference in mortality; more arrhythmias with hypothermia, reinforcing that fever prevention may be the key rather than induced hypothermia.

RCT in nonshockable rhythms that showed improved neurological outcome with hypothermia vs normothermia, extending the HACA signal to a broader population but underscoring rhythm-specific heterogeneity.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal target temperature (32–36°C) in different rhythms and risk groups?
Is the benefit of temperature control driven primarily by fever avoidance rather than active hypothermia?
What is the role of cooling in patients with initial nonshockable rhythms, longer downtimes, or older age?
How should temperature management be integrated with early coronary angiography and other post-resuscitation therapies?

numbers_to_remember: Favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1–2) at 6 months: 55% vs 39% (RR 1.40, NNT 6)
NNT for one additional favorable outcome: 6 (95% CI 3–25)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: HACA proved that temperature control after cardiac arrest can save brains and lives, but later evidence refined the target: avoid fever (≤37.5°C) rather than targeting deep hypothermia in all patients.
